title: community
aim: Look at co-living, world issues, online communities and projects that help people.
objectives: Use participle clauses to join ideas
Discuss hypothetical world issues with conditionals
Build a clear argument with prepositional phrases
Describe projects and write a mission statement

lessons.title: A new way of living
goals: Understand arguments for and against co-living
Use collocations with go, have and make

grammar.title: Participle clauses
grammar.shortAr: -ing لحدثين متزامنين، وhaving + past participle لحدث سابق، بشرط اتحاد الفاعل.
points: Use a present participle (-ing) when two actions happen at more or less the same time.
Use having + past participle when one action happened before another.
Both actions must have the same subject.
The negative forms are not + -ing and not having + past participle.
table: -ing — simultaneous actions
Moving into co-living, many people find a community.
having + past participle — earlier action
Having decided to move, they looked for a flat.
not having + past participle — negative
Not having seen him for years, I was thrilled.
not + -ing — negative reason
Not wanting to hurt him, I said nothing.
same subject required
Having finished her talk, Anna left.
exceptions: Different subjects cannot be joined in a participle clause.
Use having + past participle, not just -ing, when the first action is clearly finished.

vocab.example: Co-living offers affordable rooms and shared spaces.
Residents can use communal amenities such as a gym.
Newcomers often find a ready-made community.
The two groups rely on each other when things go wrong.
Residents have interests in common.
With the beach nearby, have a go at surfing.
He wanted to make sense of modern cities.
Things don't always go according to plan.
Architects continue working to make a difference.

reading.summary: An article weighs co-living against loneliness and high rents, describing shared facilities and flexible contracts. It also raises concerns about privacy, rules, CCTV and data privacy.

listening.summary: Recording of the article about co-living spaces and their advantages and drawbacks.
Practice noticing higher or lower pitch on participle clauses.
Vocabulary-bank practice on describing homes and living conditions.

video.summary: People give their own ideas about what the word community means.

speaking: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of each co-living space, asking partners to explain their thinking.
Say which living situation you would choose and how where you live affects your life.
writing: Write a formal application email for a role at a co-living company, covering experience, attitude and availability.

practice.q: ... to move to the city, she looked for somewhere affordable.
practice.why: The decision was completed before the search.

practice.q: ... into the building, residents immediately meet their neighbours.
practice.why: The two actions happen at almost the same time.

practice.q: ... in the neighbourhood for years, he knew everyone.
practice.why: A longer earlier state comes before the main action.

practice.q: Nothing ... according to plan, so the project is unfinished.
practice.why: The fixed phrase is go according to plan.

lessons.title: If the world ...

grammar.title: Conditionals with conjunctions
grammar.shortAr: zero / first / second / third conditional مع provided, as long as, on condition that وunless.
points: Zero conditional: if/when + present simple, present simple for general truths.
First conditional: if + present simple, will/can/may/might for future consequences.
Second conditional: if + past simple, would; formal were can replace was. Third: if + past perfect, would have.
Provided/providing (that) and as long as/so long as mean only if; on condition that is stronger; unless means if not.
table: If + present, present — general truth
If a language has no speakers, it dies.
If + present, will — future result
If we act now, many languages will survive.
If + past, would — imaginary present
If we all spoke one language, life would be easier.
If + past perfect, would have — imaginary past
If there hadn't been a campaign, Cornish would have disappeared.
as long as / unless — conditions
As long as people speak it, it will survive; unless we act, it may die.
exceptions: Unless is already negative, so do not add another negative to the same clause.
In formal second conditionals, use were instead of was.

vocab.ar: محو الأمية / القدرة على القراءة والكتابة
vocab.example: Low literacy limits access to higher education.
People want laws used with justice.
Thousands of languages are endangered.
Overcrowding is a serious problem in big cities.
Unemployment can cause many other problems.
Global warming is raising sea levels.
Homelessness means people have nowhere to live.
Poverty means people cannot afford basic needs.
People still fight for civil rights in many countries.

reading.summary: An infographic imagines the world as a village of 100 people and gives statistics about literacy, poverty, housing, languages and technology.

listening.summary: Introduction to a talk about world issues, checking the infographic statistics.
Part of the talk about endangered languages and ways of keeping them alive.
Practice identifying main stress in conditional sentences.

speaking: Choose several What if... questions and discuss their consequences with your group.
Agree or disagree with each other's predictions and explain why.
writing: Write three conditional sentences about world issues and say whether you agree with their predictions.

practice.q: If a language ... no native speakers, it dies.
practice.why: A zero conditional describes a general truth.

practice.q: If everyone ... the same language, communication would be easier.
practice.why: A second conditional uses if + past simple.

practice.q: If they ... a conscious effort, Cornish would have disappeared.
practice.why: A third conditional uses if + past perfect.

practice.q: ... we make an effort, many languages will die.

lessons.title: Online communities
goals: Recognise prepositional phrases in an article
Structure a claim, evidence and impact
Take part in a short debate

grammar.title: Developing an argument: prepositional phrases
grammar.shortAr: by far / on the whole / in fact / at least / in order to / at the same time لتنظيم الحجة.
points: Start with a claim using I'd like to start off by saying or As far as I can see.
Support it with evidence such as A good example of this is and The evidence suggests that.
Show impact with As a result, The obvious impact of this is and This would lead to.
Prepositional phrases such as by far, on the whole, in fact and at least add emphasis, generality or a minimum.
table: Making a claim
I'd like to start off by saying that I agree.
Presenting evidence
A good example of this is my local group.
Showing impact
As a result, people feel more connected.
by far — strong emphasis
It's by far the most important factor.
on the whole — generally
On the whole, online groups help local communities.
exceptions: In order to is followed by an infinitive, not an -ing form.
In fact emphasises a point, while on the whole gives a general view.

vocab.example: It is by far the most important factor.
On the whole, people enjoy online communities.
Can you name at least six neighbours?
She feared things would get out of control.
They met in order to clean the streets.
In fact, a volunteer group had already done the work.
At the same time, they were happy to help.

vocab.word: as far as I can see
vocab.example: As far as I can see, online groups are useful.

reading.summary: An article asks whether social media builds better local communities and tells how Annie Lorraine used a Facebook group after London protests. A volunteer group had already cleaned up, but many participants stayed in touch.

listening.summary: Two speakers discuss whether online communities are the best way to connect with similar people.
Grammar-bank answers for the argument-structure exercise.
Extracts practising extra stress and pauses that make an argument sound persuasive.

speaking: Split into two teams, plan arguments for and against a debate topic, then present and vote.
Use claim, evidence and impact phrases when taking turns to speak.
writing: Write a short argument about an online-community topic with a clear claim, examples and impact.

practice.q: ... the best way to build a community is to work together.
... it's easier to make friends face-to-face.
They met ... clean up the mess in the streets.
practice.why: It gives the reason or purpose.

practice.q: I'd like to start off ... saying that I agree.
practice.why: The fixed phrase is start off by saying.

lessons.title: Second shot
goals: Understand a documentary about helping homeless people
Plan and present a project and write a mission statement

grammar.title: Phrases with get
grammar.shortAr: get out / get back / get to / have got a big heart للتعبير عن الخروج من أزمة واستعادة الثقة.
points: Get out of a situation means to escape from it.
Get something back or get your confidence back means to regain what was lost.
Get to the other side or get to where you are now means to reach a goal or stage.
Have got a big heart means to be kind and generous; get a hostel means to obtain a place to live.
table: get out of — escape
It is hard to get out of homelessness.
get something back — regain
Training helps them get their confidence back.
get to the other side — reach the end
He wanted to get to the other side.
have got a big heart — be generous
Julius has got a big heart.
get somewhere / get a hostel — obtain
They have got somewhere to live now.
exceptions: Get is informal; choose a more formal verb in formal writing when appropriate.

vocab.example: It is difficult to get out of homelessness.
The cafe helps people get their life back together.
Julius helps trainees get their confidence back.
Edge believed he could get to the other side.

vocab.word: get to where you are now
vocab.example: He helped me get to where I am now.
Julius has got a big heart.
One trainee said, 'I've got a hostel now.'

vocab.word: get their lives back on track
vocab.example: The cafe helps homeless people get their lives back on track.

reading.summary: A BBC programme description introduces Julius, who opened a cafe in east London and trains homeless people as baristas to help them rebuild their lives.

listening.summary: A talk about another project that helps homeless people, with key phrases for a presentation.
Review listening to check answers in the gap-fill exercises.

video.summary: A documentary follows Julius and his cafe, which trains homeless people as baristas.

speaking: Plan a project to help people in need, then present it to the class using the key phrases.
Say which project is best and give reasons.
writing: Write a mission statement summarising a project's aims and values.

practice.q: The training helps people ... their confidence ...
practice.why: It means to regain something they lost.

practice.q: He had to work hard to ... the other side.
practice.why: It means to reach the end of a difficult situation.

practice.q: Julius is kind and generous: he's ...
practice.why: This idiom describes a generous person.

practice.q: One of the biggest problems ... homelessness.
practice.why: This is a useful opening phrase for a project presentation.

review.summary: Review participle clauses, conditional conjunctions, argument language and get phrases while recycling community and world-issue vocabulary.
tasks: Choose the correct participle form and finish a short story about an unexpected meeting.
Rewrite conditional sentences with unless, provided that and on condition that.
Prepare a short talk on a community problem using claims, evidence and impact.

... in the industry for thirty years, I know that isn't true.

If we ... left on time, we wouldn't have been late.
